entities.name: hazard analysis and critical control points
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points (HACCP) represents a paradigm shift in food safety protocols, originating in the United States during the 1960s and gaining global traction in the following decades. Developed by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) in collaboration with Pillsbury, HACCP was initially created to ensure the safety of food for astronauts, thus underscoring the importance of systematic preventive approaches to food safety. As food production expanded and global supply chains became more intricate, HACCP emerged as a fundamental framework that transcended national boundaries and regulatory environments, reshaping food safety practices worldwide.

The HACCP framework is built upon seven core principles, including conducting hazard analyses, identifying critical control points, and establishing critical limits for each point. Its application has led to significant improvements in food safety standards, with countries adopting HACCP-based regulations to mitigate risks associated with biological, chemical, and physical hazards. By the late 1990s, HACCP had been endorsed by numerous international bodies, including the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), further solidifying its role in global food safety governance.

The legacy of HACCP has been profound, influencing food safety legislation and practices across various sectors, including agriculture, food processing, and catering. Countries around the world have implemented HACCP protocols, resulting in a measurable decrease in foodborne illnesses and outbreaks. The principles of HACCP have also paved the way for modern food safety systems that prioritize preventive measures over reactive ones, demonstrating a significant shift in how societies approach public health and safety in food production.
